title: Cash Drawer Maintenance: Cleaning & Adjusting for a Longer Life
description: Sticky trays, worn springs, and dust slow down every shift. Simple cash drawer care that keeps tills opening fast for years.
body:
A cash drawer that sticks, jams, or won't pop open doesn't just annoy your cashier—it slows down every single transaction and tells customers the place is falling apart. The good news is that most drawer problems are preventable with a few minutes of routine care. Here's how to keep yours opening fast and reliably for years, without buying a replacement.

Why drawers fail in the first place

Cash drawers are simple machines: a spring-loaded latch holds the drawer shut until a pulse from your POS sends a solenoid to release it. Almost every failure traces back to one of three causes:

  • Dust and debris in the slide rails and latch, which creates friction and makes the drawer stick.
  • Worn or misaligned springs that no longer return the drawer to a closed position cleanly.
  • Coin and bill buildup wedged into the corners of the tray, which throws off the tilt and jams the mechanism.

None of these require a technician. They require a regular cleaning habit.

A 10-minute monthly cleaning routine

Set aside ten minutes once a month, ideally during a slow stretch, and work through these steps in order:

1. Empty the drawer completely

Take out every coin cup, bill clip, and the removable insert tray. This is the only way to see what's actually lodged underneath.

2. Vacuum, don't blow

Use a small vacuum or canned air to clear dust from the rails, the latch, and the rear where the solenoid sits. Avoid blowing debris deeper into the mechanism. Wipe the rails with a dry or lightly damp cloth—skip the lubricants unless the manufacturer explicitly calls for one, since grease attracts dust and makes the problem worse over time.

3. Check the springs and latch

Look at the latch spring and the return spring on the drawer body. If either looks stretched, bent, or rusty, it's a low-cost part worth replacing now rather than mid-rush. Tighten any screws on the drawer body that have worked loose.

4. Test before you reload

Close the empty drawer and trigger it from the POS a few times. It should pop open with a clean, single motion and close without resistance. If it sticks empty, reloading coins won't fix it.

Adjusting the tray so it opens right

A common complaint is a drawer that opens slowly or partially. Before blaming the solenoid, check how the coins are sitting. Overfilled coin cups tilt and press against the drawer frame, which is exactly what makes a drawer feel sluggish. A few adjustments make a real difference:

  • Keep coin cups no more than three-quarters full, and roll or deposit excess change regularly.
  • Make sure large bills are fully seated under the bill clips, not resting on the rim.
  • If your drawer has an adjustable tilt lever, set it so the front sits slightly higher than the rear—this lets gravity help the drawer close cleanly.

When a drawer is beyond a quick fix

Some symptoms mean the drawer needs a part or a replacement rather than a wipe-down. If you hear a loud click but the drawer won't release, the solenoid or its connection is likely the issue. If the drawer opens on its own or won't stay latched, the latch is worn out. If the rails are visibly bent or the drawer grinds even when empty, the frame has taken damage. These are mechanical failures, not maintenance gaps—and replacing the drawer is often cheaper than chasing a repair.

Keep your till moving

The takeaway is simple: an empty-drawer vacuum, a spring check, and a quick test once a month will keep your cash drawer opening fast through thousands of transactions. When a drawer is genuinely worn out or you're outfitting a new register, a quality drawer pays for itself in speed and fewer frustrated customers.
